question:
Distinct points \(A\) and \(B\) are on a semicircle with diameter \(MN\) and center \(C.\) The point \(P\) is on \(CN\) and \(\angle CAP=\angle CBP=10^\circ.\) If \(\overset{\frown}{MA}=40^\circ,\) then \(\overset{\frown}{BN}\) equals

[Figure 1](figures/1983_AMC_12_Q30_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The equal angles \(\angle CAP\) and \(\angle CBP\) both look toward segment \(CP\). This suggests using a second circle, separate from the given semicircle.

First, \(P\ne C\), since otherwise \(\angle CAP=0^\circ\). Also, \(P\ne N\): the given arc makes \(\angle ACN=140^\circ\), so the equal-radius triangle \(ACN\) has \(\angle CAN=20^\circ\). Thus \(P\) is strictly between \(C\) and \(N\). Neither \(A\) nor \(B\) is a diameter endpoint, so both lie on the same side of line \(CP\).

By the converse of the inscribed angle theorem, two points on the same side of a segment that see it under the same angle lie on one circle with its endpoints. Therefore \(A,B,C,P\) are concyclic. In triangle \(ACP\),
\[
\angle ACP=180^\circ-40^\circ=140^\circ,
\qquad
\angle APC=180^\circ-140^\circ-10^\circ=30^\circ.
\]
In the auxiliary circle, \(\angle ABC\) and \(\angle APC\) subtend chord \(AC\), so they are equal or supplementary, depending on which sides of the chord their vertices occupy. But \(CA=CB\), since both are radii of the original circle. Hence \(\angle ABC\) is a base angle of an isosceles triangle and is less than \(90^\circ\). It must therefore be \(30^\circ\), rather than \(150^\circ\).

It follows that
\[
\angle ACB=180^\circ-2(30^\circ)=120^\circ.
\]
Since \(\angle ACN=140^\circ\), the only position for \(B\) in the given semicircle with this separation from \(CA\) has
\[
\angle BCN=140^\circ-120^\circ=20^\circ.
\]
The degree measure of arc \(BN\) equals its central angle. Thus \(\overset{\frown}{BN}=20^\circ\), choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
